title: DET Writing: Write About the Photo & the Writing Sample
summary: The two DET writing tasks — a quick photo description and a longer sample universities read — and how to write clearly under time.

nodes.label: Write About the Photo
nodes.note: Describe an image in 1+ sentences (~1 min)

nodes.label: Keep writing
nodes.note: More relevant, correct text = more marks

chunks.heading: Write About the Photo — fast and specific
chunks.body: You see an image and **write at least one sentence describing it**, in about **a minute**. Write as much **accurate, relevant** English as you can in the time — name what's there, the action, and a detail. Quantity helps only if it's **correct and on-topic**.
chunks.realExample: Photo of a market? Write: 'A busy outdoor market where vendors sell fresh fruit and vegetables while shoppers browse the stalls in the afternoon sun.' One rich, correct sentence beats three vague ones.
chunks.memoryHook: Name it, the action, a detail — in correct English. Specific and accurate, fast.

chunks.heading: The Writing Sample — the one universities read
chunks.body: You write a **longer response to a prompt** (a few minutes), and this **Writing Sample is shared with the institutions** you apply to. Give it a **clear structure** — a position or main idea, one or two supporting points, a short close — so an admissions reader sees organised thinking.
chunks.realExample: Prompt about whether students should work part-time? State your view, give a reason with an example, add a brief counter-point, and conclude — a mini-essay an admissions officer will actually read.
chunks.memoryHook: The Writing Sample is read by humans. Give it a clear position + support + close.

chunks.heading: Correctness beats big words
chunks.body: The DET rewards **clear, grammatically correct, on-topic** writing over ambitious sentences full of errors. Use vocabulary you control, keep sentences complete, and **leave a few seconds to reread** for typos and agreement.
chunks.realExample: 'The students who works part time' has an error a reader notices instantly; 'Students who work part-time' is simple and correct. Choose correct-and-simple over fancy-and-flawed.
chunks.memoryHook: Correct beats clever. Use words you control, then reread for slips.

chunks.heading: Keep going — don't leave it short
chunks.body: Both tasks reward **producing enough relevant text** within the time. Don't stop early: as long as it stays **on-topic and correct**, more developed writing gives the scoring engine (and universities) more to reward.
chunks.realExample: Finished your main point with time left in the Writing Sample? Add a concrete example or a sentence addressing the other side — developed writing scores better than a short, thin answer.
chunks.memoryHook: Use the whole time. On-topic, correct, and developed beats short and safe.

recall.q: What does the 'Write About the Photo' task ask for?
recall.a: At least one sentence describing an image, written in about a minute — as much accurate, relevant English as you can.

recall.q: Why does the Writing Sample matter beyond the score?
recall.a: It's a longer response shared with the institutions you apply to, so admissions readers see your organised writing directly.

recall.q: What structure suits the Writing Sample?
recall.a: A clear main idea or position, one or two supporting points, and a short conclusion.

recall.q: What does DET writing reward more than ambitious vocabulary?
recall.a: Clear, grammatically correct, on-topic writing using vocabulary you control.

recall.q: Why keep writing until time is up (if it stays on-topic)?
recall.a: Both tasks reward producing enough relevant, correct text — developed answers give more to score than short ones.
